n: In Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, lives Cornelius, a centurion in the Italian Cohort. This chapter marks a turning point: the gospel formally opens to the Gentiles.

f.g: Caesarea Maritima, Herod the Great’s port city and Rome’s administrative center in Judea.
A Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
band = cohort, a unit of several hundred soldiers, here apparently recruited from Italy.

n: Cornelius is devout: he and his household revere God, he gives generously to the poor, and he prays regularly. He is a “God-fearer” — a Gentile who worships Israel’s God without becoming a full convert.

f.g: A term for Gentiles who attended synagogue and honored the God of Israel.
alway = always, regularly.

n: About three in the afternoon — the hour of prayer — he clearly sees in a vision an angel of God come in and call his name.

f.g: evidently = clearly, distinctly.
About 3 p.m.

n: Frightened, Cornelius asks, “What is it, Lord?” The angel says his prayers and gifts have risen before God as a memorial — God has noticed and remembered them.

f.w: come up for a memorial before God
f.g: Like the smoke of an offering rising to heaven.

n: He is told to send men to Joppa for a man named Simon Peter. Even with an angel present, Cornelius must receive the gospel through God’s authorized servant.
Peter is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea, and will tell Cornelius what he must do.

f.w: he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do

f.g: lodgeth = is staying.

n: When the angel leaves, Cornelius calls two household servants and a devout soldier among his personal attendants.

f.g: Cornelius’s faith had influenced those around him.

n: He tells them everything and sends them to Joppa, about thirty miles south.

f.g: Roughly 30–35 miles (50 km), a journey of more than a day.

n: Around noon the next day, as the messengers near Joppa, Peter goes up onto the flat roof to pray.

f.g: Flat roofs were used as quiet places for rest and prayer.
About noon.

n: He becomes very hungry, and while the meal is being prepared, he falls into a trance. God prepares Peter’s heart at the same time he prepares Cornelius.

f.g: Greek ekstasis — a vision-state in which one’s mind is caught up by God.

n: He sees heaven open and something like a large sheet, held by its four corners, being lowered to the earth.

f.w: a great sheet knit at the four corners
f.g: Some see the four corners as representing the four directions — the whole world.

n: In it are all kinds of animals, reptiles, and birds — clean and unclean mixed together under the law of Moses.
A voice says, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.”
Peter refuses: “No, Lord! I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” His words contain a contradiction — saying “no” to the Lord.

f.g: common = ritually impure, profane; forbidden under the dietary laws.

n: The voice replies, “What God has made clean, you must not call common.” The lesson is about food — and, as Peter will learn, about people.

f.w: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common

n: This happens three times, and the sheet is taken back up into heaven. Peter, who denied Jesus three times and was asked three times “Lovest thou me?”, now learns another lesson in threes.

f.g: thrice = three times.

n: While Peter is puzzling over the vision, the men from Cornelius find the house and stand at the gate. God’s timing is precise.

f.g: doubted = was perplexed, unsure of the meaning.

n: They call out, asking if Simon called Peter is staying there.

f.g: was staying there as a guest.

n: As Peter keeps thinking about the vision, the Spirit tells him three men are looking for him.
The Spirit says to go down and go with them without hesitation, because the Spirit himself sent them.

f.g: Or “without discriminating” — making no distinction between Jew and Gentile.

n: Peter goes down, identifies himself, and asks why they’ve come.

f.w: I am he whom ye seek
f.g: Peter meets them openly rather than hiding behind the gate.

n: They describe Cornelius as a righteous, God-fearing man respected by the whole Jewish nation, who was directed by a holy angel to invite Peter to his house and hear his message.

f.g: just = righteous, upright.
of good reputation.

n: Peter invites these Gentiles in as his guests — itself a step across a cultural line. The next day he leaves with them, along with some believers from Joppa as witnesses.

f.w: called he them in, and lodged them
f.g: Hosting Gentiles was something many devout Jews avoided.
Six Jewish believers went along, giving multiple witnesses.

n: The day after, they arrive in Caesarea. Cornelius is waiting and has gathered his relatives and close friends — he wants others to hear too.

f.w: had called together his kinsmen and near friends

n: As Peter enters, Cornelius falls at his feet in reverence.

f.g: Bowed down in deep reverence — a gesture Peter will not accept.

n: Peter lifts him up: “Stand up; I am only a man myself.” God’s servants point worship to God alone.

f.w: I myself also am a man

n: Talking with Cornelius, Peter goes inside and finds a large gathering.

f.w: found many that were come together
f.g: A house full of Gentiles eager to hear.

n: Peter acknowledges that Jewish custom forbids close association with Gentiles, but God has shown him not to call any person common or unclean. He has understood the vision: it was about people, not just food.

f.w: an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company
f.g: Not written in the law of Moses itself, but a strong tradition about ritual purity.

f.w: I should not call any man common or unclean

n: So he came without objection when invited, and now asks why they sent for him.

f.g: gainsay = object, speak against.

n: Cornelius explains that four days earlier, while fasting and praying at three in the afternoon, a man in shining clothes stood before him.

f.w: a man stood before me in bright clothing

n: The messenger said his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered by God.
He was told to send for Peter at Simon the tanner’s house by the sea, who would speak to him.

f.w: who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee

n: He sent at once and thanks Peter for coming. Now they are all present before God, ready to hear whatever the Lord has commanded. A model of how to receive a message from God.

f.w: we all here present before God

n: Peter begins: “Now I truly understand that God shows no favoritism.” This is one of the great breakthroughs of the New Testament.

f.w: God is no respecter of persons
f.g: God does not show partiality based on nationality or status.

n: In every nation, anyone who reveres God and does what is right is acceptable to him.
Peter summarizes the message God sent to Israel: the good news of peace through Jesus Christ — who is Lord of all, Jews and Gentiles alike.
They already know the story, which spread throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee after John’s baptism.

f.g: published = proclaimed, made known.

f.w: after the baptism which John preached

n: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and power. He went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him. A beautiful one-sentence summary of Christ’s ministry.

f.w: God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power

n: The apostles are witnesses of everything he did in the Jewish countryside and in Jerusalem — where they killed him by hanging him on a tree.
God raised him up on the third day and let him be seen.
Not by everyone, but by witnesses God had chosen beforehand — the apostles, who ate and drank with him after he rose. Eating with him proved his resurrected body was real.

f.w: did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead

n: He commanded them to preach and testify that he is the one God appointed to judge the living and the dead.

f.w: the Judge of quick and dead
f.g: quick = living.

n: All the prophets testify of him: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

f.w: To him give all the prophets witness

n: While Peter is still speaking, the Holy Ghost falls on all who are listening. God interrupts the sermon to settle the question. Latter-day Saints distinguish this powerful witness of the Spirit, which can come before baptism, from the gift of the Holy Ghost conferred afterward.

f.w: the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word

n: The Jewish believers who came with Peter are astonished that the Holy Ghost has been poured out even on Gentiles.

f.g: Jewish Christians.

n: They hear the Gentiles speaking in tongues and praising God — a “Gentile Pentecost.” Peter then speaks up.

f.g: magnify = praise, exalt.

n: Peter asks: can anyone refuse water to baptize these people, who have received the Holy Ghost just as we did?
He orders them baptized in the name of the Lord. They ask him to stay for some days — and Peter, once unwilling to eat with Gentiles, now lives among them.

f.w: he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord

f.g: tarry = stay. Peter would later be criticized in Jerusalem for eating with Gentiles.
